paragraphs: A counterfactual identifies a change to an input that would reverse a model’s decision. This paper studies how to find the nearest such input while making few queries to the model. Its guarantee applies to monotone models with binary outputs, and it returns an optimal counterfactual rather than merely a nearby example with a different prediction.

The key improvement changes how the number of queries depends on the problem. Previous brute-force local search required the input dimension raised to a power proportional to the distance to the nearest counterfactual. The new algorithm instead places model sensitivity inside that exponential dependence, with only a logarithmic factor in the dimension. Sensitivity measures how responsive the model is to discrete input changes.

The authors also prove a lower bound on the queries any algorithm can require. Together, the upper and lower bounds establish essentially optimal guarantees. The result makes sensitivity central to counterfactual search complexity, while retaining an exponential dependence on counterfactual distance.
icml-2022-a-query-optimal-algorithm-for-.tldr: For monotone binary models, a counterfactual search algorithm achieves essentially optimal query guarantees governed by sensitivity and counterfactual distance.

paragraphs: Clustering a network can draw on two sources of information: which nodes connect and what is known about each node. This paper investigates how to combine connections with node covariates. Its motivation is that the benefits of this additional information, and how to incorporate it optimally, are less well understood than network clustering alone.

The authors introduce an iterative clustering algorithm and establish its optimality under the Contextual Symmetric Stochastic Block Model. This model provides the setting in which the guarantee holds. The algorithm can also be applied to more general Contextual Stochastic Block Models, and it avoids the hyperparameter tuning required by previously proposed methods.

Synthetic experiments support the theoretical results and show substantial improvements over other methods. The authors also demonstrate applicability to signed graphs and examine real data. These findings establish both a model-specific optimality result and broader practical applicability; the abstract does not extend the optimality guarantee to every network on which the algorithm can run.
icml-2022-an-iterative-clustering-algori.tldr: An iterative algorithm combines network connections and node information, achieving optimality under a symmetric contextual block model without hyperparameter tuning.

paragraphs: Approximate Bayesian computation estimates uncertainty about model parameters when the likelihood is too difficult to evaluate. It commonly compares summaries of simulated data with summaries of observed data. Choosing those summaries is consequential: reducing their dimensionality can make comparison more manageable, but it can also discard information needed for useful inference.

This paper introduces an active learning approach that involves a domain expert in selecting the summary statistics. The aim is to reduce the repeated manual experimentation otherwise needed to identify suitable summaries. Expert knowledge remains part of the process, while the selection method reduces the work required to put that knowledge to use.

The authors report that expert involvement enables the method to handle misspecified models, unlike the existing dimension reduction methods they discuss. Their empirical results also show better posterior estimates than existing methods when simulations are limited. The contribution therefore concerns both the human effort involved in selecting summaries and the quality of inference achievable with a restricted simulation budget.
icml-2022-approximate-bayesian-computati.tldr: Expert-guided active learning reduces summary-statistic selection work and improves approximate Bayesian inference in experiments with limited simulations.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input belongs to the task a model was trained to handle. This paper studies detectors trained with surrogate out-of-distribution examples, which must subsequently recognize unfamiliar out-distributions. It seeks to identify shared objectives and the scoring functions implicit in methods that appear different.

The authors show that binary discrimination between in-distribution and out-of-distribution data is equivalent to several formulations of this detection problem. When trained jointly with a standard classifier, this discriminator performs similarly to Outlier Exposure. This connects a simple discrimination task to approaches presented through other training objectives.

The analysis also identifies a meaningful difference between the score implicit in Outlier Exposure’s confidence loss and the theoretically optimal score when training and test out-distributions coincide. That optimal score resembles those associated with energy-based detection and a background class. Nevertheless, matched training produces similar practical performance across these methods. The findings separate differences in theoretical scoring rules from the empirical effects observed under a shared training procedure.
icml-2022-breaking-down-out-of-distribut.tldr: Several detectors trained with out-of-distribution examples share underlying objectives and perform similarly when trained under matched conditions.

paragraphs: Explaining why an observation looks unusual does not by itself identify what caused it. This paper addresses that distinction by developing a formal method for assigning root-cause contributions to variables involved in an outlier. The target is an explanation of how variables contribute to the unusual outcome, beyond simply describing its abnormal features.

The method requires both a causal graph describing relationships among variables and a functional causal model describing those relationships. Using this causal information, it quantifies each variable’s contribution to the target outlier score. The resulting attribution expresses the extent to which each variable counts as a root cause within that model.

The authors investigate empirical performance through simulations and present an application to extreme river flows. This case study connects the formal attribution task to a real-world unusual event. The causal graph and functional model are essential inputs to the approach, so its contribution is a way to analyze outliers using an available causal description.
icml-2022-causal-structure-based-root-ca.tldr: Given a causal graph and functional causal model, the method attributes a target outlier score to contributions from individual variables.

paragraphs: Representing images through their patches has proved useful empirically. This paper supplies theoretical support by analyzing a simple semi-supervised algorithm based on patch statistics. The central result is that the algorithm can efficiently learn labels generated by a convolutional neural network with one hidden layer.

That efficiency guarantee depends on assumptions about the data distribution. Such conditions matter because learning convolutional networks is computationally difficult in the worst case. The authors show that their distributional assumptions are necessary and sufficient for their results. This identifies a setting in which patch statistics support efficient learning without claiming that every convolutional learning problem becomes easy.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 verify the stated assumptions on that dataset and find that the analyzed algorithm outperforms a vanilla one-hidden-layer convolutional network. Applying the algorithm successively across layers produces a deeper model with further improvements. The authors view this extension as suggesting insights into deep convolutional networks, while the main stated learning guarantee concerns the one-hidden-layer setting.
icml-2022-efficient-learning-of-cnns-usi.tldr: Patch statistics enable efficient learning of one-hidden-layer CNN labels under characterized distributional assumptions, with supporting CIFAR-10 results.

paragraphs: Ranking from pairwise comparisons becomes difficult when competitors differ greatly and only some pairs are observed. Winning probabilities may approach zero or one, while the pattern of available comparisons can be irregular. This paper analyzes the Bradley-Terry-Luce ranking model under these conditions, broadening settings commonly used in earlier theory.

The authors derive results about whether the maximum likelihood estimator exists and how large its estimation error can be. Their analysis allows arbitrary comparison graph structures and removes the usual requirement that winning probabilities stay bounded away from zero and one. Allowing these cases does not assert that an estimator always exists; the work characterizes conditions for its existence.

The Fisher information matrix is central to the analysis. It expresses how the comparison graph and winning probabilities jointly influence estimation risk and existence conditions. The resulting bounds recover previous results as special cases while applying more broadly. This gives a unified way to account for both uneven competition and incomplete comparisons in ranking guarantees.
icml-2022-generalized-results-for-the-ex.tldr: New Bradley-Terry-Luce estimation guarantees accommodate arbitrary comparison graphs and winning probabilities close to zero or one.

paragraphs: Second-order optimization uses curvature information in the hope of accelerating neural network training, but the relevant matrices are often too large to handle directly. KFAC makes this approach tractable through structured approximations. This paper asks whether KFAC’s practical success actually comes from closely reproducing true second-order updates.

The authors evaluate exact second-order updates and use careful ablations to examine the effects of approximation. They find that KFAC is not closely related to those updates and significantly outperforms them in their evaluation. This challenges the explanation that KFAC works well simply because it is a computationally convenient substitute for the exact procedure.

To explain the result, the authors present evidence strongly suggesting that KFAC approximates a different kind of algorithm: first-order gradient descent on neurons rather than individual weights. They also show that this optimizer often improves on KFAC in computational cost and data efficiency. The proposed connection is supported by evidence, while the reported improvements are frequent rather than universal.
icml-2022-gradient-descent-on-neurons-an.tldr: Evidence suggests KFAC’s success is better explained by neuron-level first-order optimization than by approximation of true second-order updates.

paragraphs: This paper explores learning without backpropagation in wide neural networks. It uses the Neural Tangent Kernel regime as a theoretical setting and considers such networks as a possible model of biological networks. The biological connection motivates the work, while the mathematical claims concern the specified wide-network setting.

The authors show that gradient descent produces layerwise weight updates aligned with correlations in input activity weighted by error. They also observe this alignment empirically in finite-width wide networks. The alignment provides the basis for a family of biologically motivated learning rules that avoid backpropagation and are theoretically equivalent to it in infinite-width networks.

Tests cover benchmark problems using both feedforward and recurrent networks. In wide networks, the proposed rules achieve performance comparable to backpropagation and are particularly effective when data are limited. The findings connect an infinite-width equivalence result with practical evidence at finite width. They support these alternative learning rules in the studied settings without claiming equivalence for arbitrary neural networks.
icml-2022-how-to-train-your-wide-neural-.tldr: Input–weight alignment yields backpropagation-free learning rules with infinite-width equivalence and comparable empirical performance in wide networks.

paragraphs: RETRO improves autoregressive language modeling by retrieving document chunks from an external corpus and conditioning predictions on them. Retrieval uses local similarity to the preceding tokens. This makes stored text an explicit source of information during prediction, complementing what the model has learned in its parameters.

The architecture combines a frozen BERT retriever, a differentiable encoder, and cross-attention organized around chunks. With a database containing two trillion tokens, RETRO achieves performance comparable to GPT-3 and Jurassic-1 on the Pile while using 25 times fewer parameters. The comparison concerns that evaluation; the reported parameter reduction is not a claim about every component of computational cost.

After fine-tuning, the model’s performance carries over to knowledge-intensive downstream tasks such as question answering. Although the authors typically train RETRO from scratch, they also show that pretrained transformers can quickly be fitted with retrieval and retain good performance. The work demonstrates how access to a very large explicit memory can improve language models without requiring a corresponding increase in parameter count.
icml-2022-improving-language-models-by-r.tldr: RETRO retrieves from a two-trillion-token database to match larger language models on the Pile with 25 times fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Learning an optimal Q-function is a central task in reinforcement learning: it concerns the value of taking actions when future decisions are also accounted for. This paper develops an approach based on a nonlinear Lagrangian derived from the Bellman optimality equation. It formulates optimal Q-functions through saddle points of that Lagrangian.

The main theoretical result establishes strong duality despite the Lagrangian’s nonlinearity. This provides a foundation for developing Q-function learning methods through the associated optimization formulation. The contribution therefore includes a justification for the formulation, beyond proposing a new procedure for updating value estimates.

As a demonstration, the authors derive an imitation learning algorithm from the duality theory and apply it to a machine translation benchmark. They also establish a symmetry breaking phenomenon concerning the optimality of Lagrangian saddle points. That finding motivates a direction in Lagrangian method development that the authors describe as overlooked. The abstract presents translation as an application of the theory, without claiming a particular performance improvement.
icml-2022-lagrangian-method-for-q-functi.tldr: A nonlinear Lagrangian formulation with strong duality provides a foundation for Q-function learning and an imitation learning application to translation.

paragraphs: Supervised graph prediction requires a model to output a labeled graph rather than a single number or category. This paper develops a general framework using optimal transport. It treats the task as regression with a Fused Gromov-Wasserstein loss, giving graph prediction a loss function suited to its structured outputs.

Predictions take the form of a Fused Gromov-Wasserstein barycenter, an average-like object whose weights depend on the input. The authors first introduce a nonparametric estimator based on kernel ridge regression and prove consistency and an excess-risk bound. They then develop an interpretable parametric version in which a neural network predicts the weights and the graphs being combined are learned as well.

Experiments demonstrate interpolation within the space of labeled graphs on simulated data and a difficult metabolic identification problem. The authors report strong performance on that application with little engineering. The work combines a theoretically analyzed estimator with a learned graph-combination model, making structured averaging the central mechanism for predicting graph-valued outputs.
icml-2022-learning-to-predict-graphs-wit.tldr: Optimal-transport barycenters provide a framework for graph prediction, with theoretical guarantees for one estimator and promising graph interpolation results.

paragraphs: Neural solvers for partial differential equations depend on high-quality training solutions, which usually come from the numerical solvers they aim to replace. Generating that training data therefore remains a bottleneck. This paper addresses part of the problem by improving how efficiently neural solvers learn from the available examples.

The proposed method, Lie point symmetry data augmentation, derives transformations from the symmetry group of the equation being solved. These symmetries provide a principled basis for transforming training data. In this setting, the authors can derive an exhaustive collection of transformations associated with the PDE’s Lie point symmetries, giving augmentation a mathematical connection to the governing equation.

The authors present the framework and demonstrate an order-of-magnitude improvement in neural solver sample complexity. The significance is that equation-derived transformations can make existing solution data substantially more useful for learning. The method partially alleviates dependence on expensive ground-truth generation; its stated contribution is improved data efficiency, rather than eliminating the need for training solutions.
icml-2022-lie-point-symmetry-data-augmen.tldr: Data augmentation derived from PDE symmetries demonstrates an order-of-magnitude improvement in neural solver sample complexity.

paragraphs: Estimating a mean becomes especially difficult when clean observations can have heavy tails and an adversary can arbitrarily corrupt some samples. This paper analyzes Catoni’s M-estimator under both challenges. For the uncontaminated distribution, it assumes only a known upper bound on a central moment of order one plus epsilon, with epsilon between zero and one.

The authors establish a lower bound on the worst-case mean estimation error under this assumption. They then show that the proposed estimator matches that bound up to multiplicative constants. This gives a minimax guarantee: within the analyzed setting, its error dependence cannot be substantially improved by choosing a different estimator.

The analysis also characterizes a fundamental tradeoff when variance is infinite. As epsilon approaches zero, any estimator’s tolerance to contamination decreases, and the authors provide a tight bound describing this relationship. Finally, they use the robust estimator in a bandit algorithm for partially identifiable best-arm selection, improving sample complexity over the stated existing methods.
icml-2022-minimax-m-estimation-under-adv.tldr: A robust Catoni estimator achieves minimax mean estimation rates under adversarial corruption and weak moment assumptions, up to constants.

paragraphs: This paper extends Catoni’s mean estimator to distributions that may have infinite variance. It considers independent, identically distributed real-valued observations and initially assumes a known bound on their central moment of order one plus epsilon. For epsilon below one, this assumption permits settings where a finite-variance requirement would be too restrictive.

The extension requires resolving difficulties involving roots of polynomials with degree below two. The resulting estimator preserves the order of magnitude and asymptotic constant of Catoni’s earlier result in the bounded-moment setting considered here. The authors also propose an adaptive version that learns the moment bound from data, removing the need to supply that bound in advance.

The work provides confidence bounds that apply at finite sample sizes. To demonstrate their usefulness, the authors develop best-arm identification algorithms for multi-armed bandits under a fixed-confidence requirement. They report improvements over the state of the art. The contribution links robust mean estimation under weak moment conditions to decisions that require controlled uncertainty.
icml-2022-nearly-optimal-catonis-m-estim.tldr: An extension of Catoni’s estimator handles potentially infinite variance, supports an adaptive moment bound, and improves fixed-confidence best-arm identification.

paragraphs: A generalization bound aims to connect a model’s learned behavior to its performance beyond the training data. Such a bound is useful only when it gives meaningful information. This paper derives bounds for a specific family of shallow neural networks and demonstrates cases in which the resulting guarantees are non-vacuous.

The networks have one hidden layer, use L2-normalized inputs, and employ either the Gaussian error function activation or GELU. The analysis uses PAC-Bayesian theory. A distinguishing feature is that the bounds apply to networks with deterministic parameters, unlike many existing bounds in this family that concern randomized parameters.

The authors evaluate the bounds on networks trained with ordinary stochastic gradient descent using MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. In these experiments, the bounds are informative rather than vacuous. This connects the theoretical analysis to a standard training procedure for the specified architectures. The finding concerns these restricted network and input conditions; its significance is a meaningful guarantee for deterministic trained networks within that setting.
icml-2022-non-vacuous-generalisation-bou.tldr: PAC-Bayesian bounds for specified deterministic single-hidden-layer networks are empirically non-vacuous on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST.

paragraphs: Sequential experimental design chooses experiments over a sequence of decisions. Bayesian approaches provide a principled formulation but can be computationally demanding. Earlier amortized methods address deployment cost by training a policy in advance, yet may explore inadequately and require both differentiable probabilistic models and continuous design choices.

This paper shows that optimizing the design policy can be reduced to solving a Markov decision process. The authors then apply modern deep reinforcement learning to that equivalent problem. The reformulation makes sequential experimental design accessible to policy-learning techniques that can accommodate discrete as well as continuous choices.

Experiments show efficient deployment and state-of-the-art performance in both types of design space, including cases where the probabilistic model is a black box. The result broadens the settings in which a pretrained design policy can be useful. In particular, the reported approach combines low deployment cost with the ability to work without the differentiable-model requirement of the earlier methods discussed.
icml-2022-optimizing-sequential-experime.tldr: Recasting sequential experimental design as an MDP enables efficient learned policies for continuous or discrete choices, including black-box models.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains across users by sending model updates to a central server instead of collecting entire datasets. This paper studies a personalized version with both local and global models. Its central question is how coordinating these two forms of learning affects the balance between prediction accuracy and privacy.

The analysis considers stochastic optimization under user-level joint differential privacy. In this setting, learning a private global model carries a privacy-related cost, while local learning is perfectly private. Personalization therefore provides a way to combine learning that stays with an individual user and learning that benefits from coordination across users.

The authors give generalization guarantees showing that this coordination yields a broadly useful improvement in the privacy–accuracy tradeoff. They illustrate the theory with experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets. The result positions personalization as part of the privacy mechanism’s design: deciding what to learn locally and what to learn centrally can improve the accuracy available under the studied privacy requirement.
icml-2022-personalization-improves-priva.tldr: Coordinating local personalization with private global learning improves the privacy–accuracy tradeoff under user-level joint differential privacy.

paragraphs: Decision tree methods such as ID3, C4.5, and CART have long been practical tools for machine learning. This paper investigates the theoretical basis of their ability to learn from noisy data. It treats these familiar methods as members of the broader family of impurity-based decision tree algorithms.

Using a boosting framework, the authors prove strong noise-tolerance guarantees for that family. The results hold under the nasty-noise model, described in the abstract as the strongest noise setting. They also establish nearly matching upper and lower bounds on the noise rate that can be tolerated, characterizing both achievable robustness and its limits.

The authors show that these practical algorithms have guarantees in the noisy setting that existing algorithms in the theoretical decision-tree literature do not match. The contribution is therefore a theoretical explanation for the robustness of established learning procedures. The near-matching bounds also make clear that tolerance has a quantitative boundary, rather than implying successful learning under arbitrarily large amounts of noise.
icml-2022-popular-decision-tree-algorith.tldr: A boosting-based analysis proves strong noise tolerance for impurity-based decision trees, with nearly matching bounds on allowable noise.

paragraphs: This paper studies an agent repeatedly making sequential decisions in a stochastic environment represented by a tree. Each round produces both utility and cost. The agent must learn a good strategy while keeping costs under a safety threshold, creating a tension between improving decisions and respecting constraints.

For a hard threshold, the constraint must hold at every iteration with high probability. The authors show that, in general, any algorithm providing this guarantee incurs linear regret. They therefore consider a softer requirement: cumulative threshold violations need only grow sublinearly. Under that relaxation, they provide an algorithm with sublinear regret, so average regret and average cumulative violation diminish over time.

A hard-threshold guarantee with sublinear regret becomes possible under an additional assumption: a known strategy strictly satisfies the safety constraint. The authors give an algorithm for this setting and show their regret bounds are tight. They also formulate opponent exploitation within the framework and evaluate the algorithms on a standard collection of games.
icml-2022-safe-learning-in-tree-form-seq.tldr: Sublinear-regret safe learning requires either relaxed cumulative constraints or, for strict per-round safety, a known strictly safe strategy.

paragraphs: Spike-and-slab priors support Bayesian variable selection by representing different states for regression covariates. They are valued for interpretability and statistical properties, but sampling their posterior becomes costly with many variables. This paper introduces Scalable Spike-and-Slab, or S³, a Gibbs sampling implementation for high-dimensional regression with a continuous spike-and-slab prior.

Its per-iteration cost is of order max{n²p_t, np}, where n counts observations and p counts covariates. The quantity p_t is no larger than the number of covariates switching states between successive iterations. This improves on the n²p cost of existing implementations because the number switching states is typically much smaller than the total number of covariates.

On synthetic and real-world datasets, the authors report orders-of-magnitude speedups over existing exact samplers. They also find better inferential quality than approximate samplers operating at comparable cost. The contribution makes posterior sampling more practical by connecting computational effort to changes within the sampling process, while the stated cost still includes a term involving all covariates.
icml-2022-scalable-spike-and-slab-53ad36.tldr: S³ accelerates spike-and-slab Gibbs sampling by tying much of each iteration’s cost to covariates that switch states.

paragraphs: A melanoma classifier can perform well while still relying on misleading patterns in its training images. This paper examines biases associated with visible surgical markings, rulers, and the instrument used to capture lesion images. Such influences can create irregular predictions even when convolutional networks achieve dermatologist-level classification performance.

The authors apply two leading bias-unlearning techniques within an automated melanoma classification pipeline. Their goal is to reduce the influence of these unwanted image variations on the classifier. They show that the effects of surgical markings and rulers identified in previous studies can be reasonably mitigated using the methods.

They also demonstrate generalization benefits from unlearning variation associated with the imaging instrument. Across the experiments, the effects of all three kinds of bias are notably reduced, while different techniques perform best on different tasks. These results support debiasing as a useful part of the pipeline, with evidence of mitigation rather than a claim that the studied biases have been completely eliminated.
icml-2022-skin-deep-unlearning-artefact-.tldr: Two bias-unlearning methods reduce melanoma classifiers’ sensitivity to image artifacts and imaging instruments, with different strengths across tasks.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial networks learn distributions through competition between a generator and a discriminator. This paper develops a framework for distributions with additional structure, such as group symmetry. It introduces new variational representations of distribution divergences so that this structure can be incorporated into the learning problem.

The theory shows how to project the discriminator space onto an invariant space using conditional expectation associated with the structure. It also proves that reducing the discriminator space must be paired with careful generator design: flawed structured generators can lead to severe mode collapse. The two components therefore need coordinated treatment.

For distributions with group symmetry, the authors build models combining an equivariant generator and an invariant discriminator, demonstrating distinct roles for each. Experiments and ablations across datasets, including medical images, support the theory. Reported improvements in sample quality and diversity include nearly an order-of-magnitude improvement measured by Fréchet Inception Distance, especially with little data. The findings connect structural design choices to more effective learning in that regime.
icml-2022-structure-preserving-gans-a9ce.tldr: Structure-preserving GANs coordinate invariant discriminators and structured generators to improve sample quality and diversity, especially with limited data.

paragraphs: Recovering a nonlinear dynamical system from observed time series is difficult when noise and chaotic behavior are present. Deep learning models can also require large latent spaces that make the recovered dynamics hard to analyze. This paper seeks richer modeling capacity while retaining a comparatively compact and mathematically tractable representation.

Inspired by principles of dendritic computation, the authors add a linear spline basis expansion to a piecewise-linear recurrent neural network. They show that the expanded model retains the appealing theoretical properties of the original architecture while improving its capacity to approximate arbitrary nonlinear dynamical systems in relatively low dimensions.

The authors train the model through two frameworks: backpropagation through time combined with teacher forcing, and fast, scalable variational inference. On dynamical-system benchmarks, the expanded network produces better reconstructions with fewer parameters and dimensions and compares favorably with other methods. The result links increased expressive capacity to a structure that remains interpretable and tractable, rather than relying solely on larger latent representations.
icml-2022-tractable-dendritic-rnns-for-r.tldr: A spline-expanded recurrent network improves dynamical-system reconstruction with fewer parameters and dimensions while retaining mathematical tractability.

paragraphs: Stochastic volatility models describe changing variability through systems of stochastic differential equations. They have been successful in areas including finance and statistical climatology, but typically lack a way to condition on historical observations to obtain a true posterior distribution. This paper addresses that gap for a class of these models.

The authors recast the models as hierarchical Gaussian processes with specialized covariance functions. This preserves the original models’ inductive biases while enabling Gaussian process inference to produce a posterior predictive distribution. The reformulation therefore connects assumptions about changing volatility with a framework that explicitly incorporates observed data into forecasts and their uncertainty.

Within this framework, the authors introduce Volt and Magpie, drawing inspiration from established application domains. They report that the models significantly outperform baselines in stock and wind-speed forecasting and naturally extend to multitask prediction. The contribution combines a probabilistic reformulation with evidence of forecasting improvements in these two settings, rather than claiming that every stochastic volatility model admits the same construction.
icml-2022-volatility-based-kernels-and-m.tldr: Volt and Magpie recast stochastic volatility modeling through Gaussian processes, enabling posterior forecasts and improving stock and wind-speed prediction.
